source.title: Efficiency at What Cost? Safety and Fairness in Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of LLMs
source.authors: M. Taraghi; Y. Pequignot; Amin Nikanjam; Mohamed Amine Merzouk; F. Khomh

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Its displayed title differs from the supplied title; no missing or garbled sections prevent extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether benign fine-tuning changes harmful-request safety, using PEFT methods and safety measures rather than the original study’s fine-tuning setup.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates harmful-request safety after benign conversational and coding fine-tuning. Its safety results bear on V2. It does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, test compliant-prefill/suffix/decoding bypasses, isolate safety-carrying parameters, explain first-token shallowness, or test methods designed to deepen safety. The safety figures and extensive category-level statistical tables contain additional results, but many individual values are not stated in the text or are not extractable from the supplied flattened text.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes four safety-tuned or instruct 7–8B models on benign data (UltraFeedback, UltraChat, CodeAlpaca). It uses four PEFT methods and reports HEx-PHI harmful-request safety change against each base model. That bears directly on V2. Measure and benchmark overlap Qi et al., but the judge (LLaMA-Guard 2) and the PEFT families differ, so this is a different method aimed at the same question. No harmful data, KL, prefill, localization or deepening tests appear, so V1 and V3–V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that benign PEFT can materially shift safety and fairness, depending mainly on PEFT family and base model. Adapter methods (LoRA, IA3) preserve or significantly improve safety; prompt-based methods significantly degrade it. LLaMA is stable, Qwen gains modestly, Gemma declines most, and Mistral is volatile. The aggregate safety change is non-significant. CodeAlpaca also lowers safety versus base, with no significant safety difference from matched conversational runs.
record.recipe_differences: Tests benign PEFT (LoRA, IA3, Prompt-Tuning, P-Tuning) on four instruction-tuned 7–8B model families, with HEx-PHI safety evaluation; includes SFT and DPO conversational settings and a conservative SFT CodeAlpaca extension. It does not test harmful fine-tuning examples.
record.method_sensitivity: Safety outcomes vary by PEFT method and base model. The paper reports prompt-based methods as more safety-degrading overall, with Gemma significantly degrading and Qwen improving on average. Targeted sensitivity results show safety changes across LoRA ranks and prompt virtual-token counts; GPT-4.1 and LLaMA-Guard 2 have similar method ordering, though their unsafe rates differ.

fits_no_version.finding: Benign PEFT significantly degrades BBQ-Lite fairness accuracy and raises bias magnitude, especially for prompt-based methods; IA3 is most robust.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign fine-tuning erodes fairness/bias alignment as well as refusal safety.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-4.1 and LLaMA-Guard 2 unsafe rates correlate strongly (Pearson r=0.946) and preserve the same method ordering.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to four instruction-tuned models of 7–8B parameters and selected datasets/configurations. Safety is measured by automated judges; the main evaluation uses LLaMA-Guard 2, with GPT-4.1 checked only on a selected subset. Ten fine-tuned models with inference failures and 19 utility outliers were removed. Three repeats were averaged. The aggregate safety decrease was not statistically significant; many finer-grained safety values are figure-based or only summarized qualitatively. The paper itself notes limited generalization beyond its single coding dataset and conservative SFT settings.
record.rows_left_out: Did not transcribe figure-only safety values from Figs. 1–5 or the large category-level statistical tables in Appendices G. These contain numerous category-by-method/model comparisons, but the supplied text does not expose their individual safety change values in a reliably assignable form. Main text’s qualitative category and method summaries are included in R6.

untested.parts: Full-parameter fine-tuning; few-example regimes (training sets were about 20K examples); identity-shifting or specially selected benign data; models beyond 7–8B.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefill, suffix or decoding attacks.
No test of safety localization in weights or ranks. LoRA rank is varied only as a fine-tuning hyperparameter.
No test of why alignment is shallow.

missing.what: Per-method significance versus base: adapter methods give statistically significant safety gains; Prompt-Tuning and P-Tuning give significant regressions (Findings summary 1; Table XIV, method-vs-base rows).
missing.locator: Section IV-A Findings summary; Table XIV

missing.what: Category-level overall changes: Child Abuse, Fraud/Deception, Adult Content and Privacy Violation decline significantly; Malware increases significantly.
Base-model safety scores per model and category, the baselines for all rows (e.g., LLaMA 93.94, Gemma 92.12, Qwen 83.94, Mistral 55.15).
Training-variable effects: 1 vs 5 epochs, learning rate, dataset, and SFT vs DPO all show small safety differences (DPO SD 3.45 vs SFT 9.85).
CodeAlpaca category-level significant declines in 9 hazard categories versus base; no significant safety difference versus matched UltraFeedback runs.
IA3 sensitivity: safety change +0.983 (q,v,down) vs +0.909 (k,v,down) relative to base.

record.verdict_notes: Verdicts rest on LLaMA-Guard 2 scoring of HEx-PHI. Mistral-7B-Instruct had no safety tuning per its model card, so its rows bear only weakly on 'eroding' safety. Results are base-relative averages after removing 10 failed models and 19 utility outliers, which may understate worst-case erosion. The sensitivity rows (R7–R15) come from one slice (UltraFeedback SFT, lr 2e-5, 5 epochs) with no per-setting significance tests.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful fine-tuning data are used; the training data are described as benign.
The study tests selected benign PEFT datasets and settings, not the full range of ordinary or carefully chosen benign datasets or the specific few-to-few-hundred-example regime.
No per-token KL divergence or response-position analysis.
No compliant-opening prefills, suffix attacks, or decoding changes are tested.
PEFT and rank sensitivity are evaluated, but the study does not test whether safety is localized in a small set of parameters or ranks.
No test of whether data or training objectives produce first-token shallowness.
No training designed to spread safety across response positions and no test of whether such deepening holds up.
